Build Step 1 of the Build Comparison project it describes: research with verified facts first, then design, build, adversarial review rounds with fixes, and publish. Use workflows for the research and review rounds, modelled on history/scratchpad/workflows/.

Rex and Ollie's A-pose turnarounds are in build-comparison/assets/. Use them as the style key and for their outlines only; their mass stays as is until Step 2.

Work on a claude/ branch. Update STATUS.md as you go, push regularly, and open a pull request when it's ready for review. Don't merge it yourself. If you need an art asset, describe exactly what you need and keep going without it until I reply. Finish with a history/ entry for this session, like the existing one.

I'm going to bed, so get as far as you can.

facts: 18 (8 derived, 7 reported, 2 measured, 1 disputed).
Topic: a muscle index that does not depend on size. I fetched 20 sources: Europe PMC abstract records, full texts of Heymsfield 2007, Peterson 2017 and Burton 2018 from PMC, Haldane's essay, Galileo via a UVa lecture page, plus Harper's archive metadata.

args.prompt:
Project: "Build Comparison", a chart that ranks male body builds by "muscle level" irrespective of height, from ordinary men through the limits of human possibility to the monstrous (comic characters, and two original 3 m characters, Rex and Ollie). Read /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-comparison/BRIEF.md first (10 minutes): it states the decisions already made and the problems to solve.
The working score is FFMI after rescaling the body to 1.80 m at the same shape: S = 1.8 * FFM / H^3 (FFM = fat-free mass in kg, H = height in m), shown beside plain FFMI = FFM / H^2. A rough first pass gives: US Army median man about 24, Ronnie Coleman about 35-39, Eddie Hall about 38, the heaviest comic characters 57-81, Rex about 141 (tail excluded, height to crest). A solid ball of muscle as tall as the figure scores about 924.
The sister project /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-calculator/ already holds 55 builds and 139 verified facts in data/builds.json (read its "facts" keys and labels before you start; do NOT re-research a fact that already exists there unless the brief needs a number it lacks, and say so when you rely on an existing key). ANSUR II CSVs are in /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-calculator/data/ansur2/ (ANSUR_II_MALE_Public.csv, 4,082 men; values in mm and kg x10? check: weightkg is in tenths of kg, lengths in mm).
The owner is a professional critic: factual accuracy and honest labelling come first. Say "unknown" rather than invent; a number is "sourced" only if you fetched the page or PDF and saw the number there; give the exact URL you fetched (DOI landing pages, PubMed, PMC, publisher PDFs). Prefer primary or authoritative sources (journals, textbooks, government surveys, standards bodies, publisher handbooks); use fan sites or magazines only when nothing better exists, and label them so. Quote the exact sentence or table cell behind each number in notes.
Load web tools with ToolSearch query "select:WebSearch,WebFetch". Write raw downloads and scripts under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-rex-strength-lab/9b81b796-3162-56bd-85b7-22e02b6583e2/scratchpad/research/<topic>/ (create it). Do not edit anything under /home/user/rex-strength-lab.
For each fact give: key (snake_case), label, status (measured | official | reported | derived | estimate | disputed), values (a JSON object as a string, SI units plus the original units), sources (title + URL actually fetched), and notes (what exactly the source says, its sample, caveats, how good the evidence is).

TOPIC: a size-independent muscle index. (1) Confirm the definition of FFMI (VanItallie et al. 1990, Am J Clin Nutr) and Kouri et al. 1995's normalisation to 1.80 m (exact formula and constant as printed). (2) Sources for geometric similarity: at the same shape, mass scales with length cubed (isometric scaling; e.g. Schmidt-Nielsen 1984 "Scaling: why is animal size so important?", McMahon 1973 Science, Haldane "On being the right size", Galileo square-cube law); find a fetched, citable statement. (3) Indices that divide by height cubed: Rohrer's index / ponderal index (Rohrer 1921) and any published fat-free-mass-over-height-cubed index (e.g. Wells & Cole 2002 Int J Obes on adjusting FFM for height in children; any "FFM/H^3" or "lean mass index with power 3" in the literature). (4) How FFM actually scales with height in adult humans (Heymsfield et al. 2007 AJCN exists in builds.json as heymsfield_2007_scaling; check what else exists: e.g. VanItallie, Schutz 2002, Kouri's own exponent); explain why plain FFMI is roughly height-independent among humans but grows in proportion to height for a body scaled up at the same shape. (5) Is there a better-sourced choice than 1.8*FFM/H^3 for comparing bodies of very different heights at the same shape? Look for allometry-based recommendations. Recommend, with sources, and state where the rescaled index stops being valid (e.g. it ignores that real tall humans are not scaled copies; Kouri's correction is fitted only to human heights). Compute and report, as derived facts: the rescaled index for a 1.80 m man equals plain FFMI; for the same shape scaled to 3.048 m plain FFMI is 3.048/1.8 = 1.693 times larger.

TOPIC: where extreme muscle stops a body working. The chart will mark, by 2D geometry on drawn front-view silhouettes whose widths are scaled up at fixed height, three functional limits: (a) the arms can no longer hang down by the sides, (b) the thighs touch all the way to the knee, (c) the hands can no longer reach the face. Find sources that make these definitions defensible: (1) soft-tissue approximation as the end-feel limiting elbow flexion and knee flexion (Norkin & White "Measurement of Joint Motion", Kapandji, Magee "Orthopedic Physical Assessment", AAOS norms); normal active elbow flexion range (about 140-150 degrees) and what limits it. (2) Functional elbow range for daily tasks, especially hand-to-mouth, eating, reaching the face and head (Morrey, Askew & Chao 1981 J Bone Joint Surg Am 63:872; Sardelli et al. 2011 J Bone Joint Surg Am; Oosterwijk et al. 2018 review; Raiss et al. 2007); give the elbow flexion angle each task needs. (3) Evidence that very large muscle mass reduces range of motion (studies of bodybuilders' or powerlifters' flexibility and joint range, e.g. Chang, Buschbacher & Edlich 1988 "Limited joint mobility in power lifters"; any study measuring elbow flexion or shoulder adduction in bodybuilders); and shoulder adduction or the arm-against-torso contact (lat spread). (4) Inner-thigh contact: any anthropometric source on thigh contact or the "thigh gap" in men, and the standing stance used in anthropometry (ANSUR II standing posture: heels together or feet apart?). (5) Joint geometry needed: elbow flexion stops when forearm and upper-arm soft tissue meet; give sources or models that compute maximum flexion from limb cross-section (e.g. in biomechanics or ergonomics, CAD human models such as Jack or RAMSIS, or soft-tissue collision in animation papers). Recommend precise, citable definitions and thresholds for (a), (b), (c), say what each ignores (3D shape, tissue compression, posture), and label every threshold as an estimate.

(1) The height slope is 6.1 kg/m³ in the methods. The abstract prints 6.3. This settles the two keys marked "disputed".

(2) The pre-steroid Mr America winners were not given an assumed 5% fat. Pope estimated each man's fat blind from magazine photographs, and later recalled estimates of about 6–16%. - Users: 83 men, spread from 19 to 31.9. 37 were at or above 25 and 2 were above 30.

Data behind it:
- fitmatic (secondary): 'approximately 300 natural bodybuilding champions spanning from 1947 to 2010'.
- Butt's own sister article (reposted): 'a similar 6-year study I did on champion bodybuilders', based on 'drug-free champions both past and present'.

Peer review and validation: none found. Label: "heaviest measured fat-free mass; drug status not reported; high body fat inflates FFM". Kondo's proposed 0.7 kg/cm (S 38.9 at 1.80 m) is an extrapolation; give it in text only, or as a hollow marker. Hattori's top-division sumo cut-off, FFMI about 30, can go in the details.

3. Conversion method, to state on the page:
   - At 1.80 m, plain FFMI = Kouri-normalised = Trexler-normalised = S.
   - Otherwise, plain F = N − k(1.8 − H), with k = 6.1 for Kouri and 2.943 for Trexler; then S = 1.8F/H.
   - Plot published normalised values at their 1.80 m basis. Where a sample's heights are unknown, say so.
   - Add a footnote that S assumes fat-free mass grows with height cubed, while Kouri's data imply about height to the power 2.4. So on S, short natural lifters score up to about 1.5 units higher and tall ones about 1 unit lower.

4. Body-fat caveat beside the band: fat-free mass rises with fat (Kouri's own fourth limitation, the sumo data, and builds.json ffmi_obesity_caveat). High-fat samples (football linemen, sumo) overstate muscle.

5. Keep off the chart, mention in the notes: McDonald's and Aragon/Helms's models are rates of gain from experience, not ceilings, and cannot be converted without a starting mass and a height. Schoenfeld: no model found.

6. Enhanced-region anchor available from the same paper: Kouri's 33 magazine bodybuilders, 1989–94, at an assumed 5% fat. Normalised FFMI from 26 to just under 40, mean about 31.5.

7. Update builds.json as listed in builds_json_kouri_corrections:
   - k = 6.1, no longer disputed.
   - Mr America fat came from blind photo estimates, not 5%.
   - Non-users' fat was 12.5 ± 5.5%.
   - The top user is in the 31–31.9 bin, not 32.
   - Normalisation strings say 6.1.",
 "gaps": "Kouri 1995:
- The exact top non-user value is not printed. Fig. 2 places it between 24.0 and 24.9, and the text says "<25.0".
- Individual non-user heights and FFMIs are not given.
- Kouri's per-man heights, weights and body-fat estimates for the Mr Americas were never published (Todd 2008 says Pope confirmed this). Converting them to S used Todd's heights, which is an estimate.

Casey Butt:
- The primary pages (weightrainer.net) are dead: the domain is parked.
- The Wayback Machine was blocked by the egress policy, and archive.ph reset the connection. The formula comes from two secondary calculators. It reproduces exactly the three Butt-calculator outputs McDonald published, which is strong but indirect confirmation.
- I did not consult the book "Your Muscular Potential". The only copy found was an unauthorised forum upload.
- The "about 300 champions, 1947–2010" sample is secondary (fitmatic). Butt's PhD field is unverified.
- The girth equations come from a forum repost of his free article.

Abstracts only (paywalled):
- Kondo 1994, Abe 2018, Abe 2020, Hattori 1999 and Currier 2019. Not known from these: the sports in Abe's sample, any athlete heights or FFMI values, Currier's regression slope, reference height, maximum and drug testing.
- Hattori's mean of 26.6 and maximum of about 37 come via Trexler's citation.
- The NFL DXA paper (Dengel 2014) gives no numbers in its abstract and was not used.

Rate models:
- I did not find the Aragon/Helms percentage-per-month table in a primary Aragon or Helms source; it is McDonald's attribution. Aragon's own 2011 interview gives pounds per year.
- Schoenfeld: no frame-based or ceiling model found. The Human Kinetics page a search pointed to now redirects to a homepage.

Drug testing:
- I found no peer-reviewed study that reports FFMI above 28 in athletes under documented individual drug testing.
- Trexler relies on NCAA random testing and did no testing of its own.
- The one sample that required negative tests (Santos 2014) tops out at a 95th percentile of about 26.
- Sumo papers do not mention testing.

Small inconsistencies, all noted in the facts:
- Todd's text says 18 men above 25 and a mean of 26.54 for 20 men. Her table gives 17 and 26.46.
- Two of Todd's rows do not reproduce from her rounded fat column.
- Kouri's Fig. 3 and Table 2 differ by one man between the 22 and 24 bins.
- Kouri prints "67%" for 52/83, which is 63%.

Cross-check for the parent, outside this topic:
- The brief's first-pass ANSUR II median of about 24 on S needs about 15% fat. The median soldier is 1.755 m and 84.6 kg; S is 22.5 at 20% fat and 23.9 at 15%.
- That would put an average soldier above the mean of Kouri's 74 trained non-users (plain FFMI 21.8), so the assumed fat deserves a check."

 "summary": "I covered all five parts of the outline topic.

**(1) Measurement definitions.** I downloaded the ANSUR II measurer's handbook (Hotzman 2011, TR-11/017) and the methods report (Gordon 2014, TR-15/007) and quoted the exact definition and posture for every landmark height and breadth on the list, with printed page numbers.
- Chest breadth is taken at full inspiration, with the caliper pressed "firmly to ensure contact with the rib cage". The handbook never mentions the latissimus. So chest breadth is a squeezed rib-cage width, not a silhouette width.
- Biacromial breadth runs between the bony acromion tips. Bideltoid breadth is the widest point across the deltoid muscles of the arms. Both are measured seated. In ANSUR men the median gap is 47 mm per side.

**(2) Limb cross-section shape.** ANSUR II has no limb breadths or depths. The AIST 1991-92 database (217 Japanese men aged 18–29, a government survey) does. It gives breadth, depth and girth at one level for the thigh, knee, calf and ankle:
- Thigh and calf are close to round (depth/breadth 1.02 and 0.98).
- The knee is deeper than wide (1.09) and the ankle more so (1.25).
- In all four, an ellipse built from breadth and depth comes within 2–5% of the girth.

The upper arm is clearly not round. In Liu 2018, a circle from one photo view misses the arm girth by 17–20%, while an ellipse from front and side views gets within about 3%. Heymsfield 1982 (CT) agrees. Neither source says which view is wider.

The cadaver studies named in the task (Clauser 1969, Chandler 1975, McConville 1980) could not be reached: DTIC blocked them. Dempster 1955 sits behind a Cloudflare challenge.

**(3) Joint centres.** De Leva 1996 Table 2 is fetched and verified. It places the shoulder joint centre 34.5 mm below the acromion, the hip centre 3.2 mm above trochanterion, and the knee centre 33.5–35 mm above tibiale; the elbow, wrist and ankle offsets are in the fact. These come from Chandler's six cadavers.
- Hara 2016 (CT of 157 bodies, open access) gives hip-centre regressions accurate to 4–5 mm. Bell's equations err by 6–11 mm on the same data.
- A small elderly radiograph study (Hu 2022) supports the hip centre sitting level with the top of the greater trochanter (median 6 mm).
- For the shoulder, only abstracts were reachable (Meskers 1998, Campbell 2009, Rab 2002), plus Vicon's guideline. The ISB recommendations are paywalled; I fetched only their abstracts.

| Site | Girth / ellipse (mean ± SD) | Trend with build |

| Chest | 1.238 ± 0.032 | rises from 1.22 to 1.26 across BMI fifths |
| Waist (navel) | 1.054 ± 0.018 | flat |

- Shoulder = acromial height - 0.104 x acromion-radiale.
- Elbow = acromial height - acromion-radiale + 0.0431 x acromion-radiale. Radiale height is not in ANSUR II, so it is approximated with the arm hanging.

 "recommendations": "**Status labels on the chart**
- Measurement definitions: "official".
- ANSUR and AIST fractions: "derived" (ratios of measured data).
- Joint centres: "reported" or "derived".
- Upper-arm and neck widths, and anything past ANSUR's range: "estimate" or "template".

**1. Template heights.** Draw every human build on one template from ANSUR II median fractions of stature: crown 1.000, chin about 0.871 (estimate), cervicale 0.864, acromion 0.821, suprasternale 0.819, axilla 0.757, chest point 0.735, waist (omphalion) 0.602, trochanterion 0.512, buttock 0.505, crotch 0.481, wrist 0.4825, fingertip 0.373, knee (midpatella) 0.278, lateral malleolus 0.0415. Keep these fixed for every build, since they vary little (SD 0.003–0.016). Only widths change with build. The template is a relaxed arms-down stance; an A-pose rotates the arms about the shoulder centre.

**2. Trunk widths from girths.** Use ANSUR ratios.

| Site | Front width / girth | Side depth / girth | Effective ellipse width / girth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chest | 0.274 | 0.240 | 0.388 |
| Waist (navel) | 0.348 | 0.252 | 0.379 |
| Buttock / hip | 0.339 | 0.241 | 0.387 |

Chest breadth is a squeezed rib-cage width, so it is narrower than the visible torso. For a filled outline whose ellipse must match the girth, use about 0.38–0.39 × girth as the torso width at all three sites, with the measured depth.
- The ratios drift with build: chest width/girth falls from 0.288 in the leanest fifth to 0.261 in the heaviest. Show this drift as the uncertainty band.
- For bodybuilders and comic figures, hold the ANSUR ratios and label the outline "template".

**3. Limbs (AIST data).**
- Thigh at the gluteal furrow and calf at its widest are close to round: width ≈ depth ≈ 0.31 × girth (girth ≈ π × width).
- Knee: width 0.295 × girth, depth 0.323 × girth.
- Ankle: width 0.267 × girth, depth 0.335 × girth.
- Forearm (palms forward): width ≈ 0.36 × relaxed girth. Narrower with palms in.
- Upper arm: not round (aspect roughly 0.55–0.7), and no source says which way. Draw it from girth/π and label it estimate, about ±15%.
- Neck: no shape data. Use girth/π and label it estimate.

**4. Measuring tool (girth from front width × side depth).**
- Limbs: the ellipse is good to about 2–5% (thigh 2.3%, calf and knee 3%, ankle 5%, upper arm about 3% in Liu 2018).
- Trunk: multiply the Ramanujan ellipse by site factors. Waist ×1.054 (±0.036 at 2 SD), buttock ×1.090 (±0.039), head ×1.029.
- Chest: ×1.24 applies only to rib-cage-style widths. For outline widths that include the lats, flag the result as unvalidated and quote at least ±10%.
- This supports the brief's stated 5–10% girth uncertainty.

**5. Joint centres for posing and for the "body stops working" limits.**
- Shoulder: 0.104 × acromion–radiale length below the acromion (about 35 mm, 0.020 of stature, at 0.801 of stature), on the upper arm's axis.
- Elbow: about 0.638 of stature.
- Wrist: wrist height.
- Hip: at trochanterion height (0.514), each about 0.05 of stature from the midline (inter-hip distance about 0.10 of stature, about half the hip breadth; estimate).
- Knee: lateral femoral epicondyle height (0.280 to 0.2845).
- Ankle: lateral malleolus height.
- For the arms-hang test, the ANSUR median room per side is (bideltoid − biacromial)/2 = 47 mm and (bideltoid − chest breadth)/2 = 110 mm. Compare these with the drawn upper-arm width.

**6. Head, hands and feet.**
- Head height about 0.13 of stature (7.2–7.8 heads); breadth 0.088; length 0.114 (length/breadth 1.30).
- Hand length 0.110, breadth 0.050, thickness 0.016. With palms in, the front view shows thickness.
- Foot length 0.154, breadth 0.058, instep height 0.036, ankle 0.0415.
- Simplify hands to mitts and feet to wedges at these sizes, matching the turnaround style.

**7. Cite existing keys rather than duplicating them.** Use `ansur2_segments_male`, `trunk_cross_section_shape`, `ezone_volume_accuracy` and `inertia_model_mass_accuracy_table`, and point to these new keys for the spreads and limb shapes.",
 "gaps": "**Paywalled; only abstracts or records fetched**
- ISB recommendations (Wu 2002 Part I, Wu 2005 Part II): abstracts contain no joint-centre definitions. The "midpoint of the epicondyles" rule for elbow and knee is therefore not verified from the ISB text.
- Bell 1990: record only, so its equations are not verified. Only its errors on Hara's CT data are quoted.
- Harrington 2007: abstract only, so its equations are not quoted.
- Meskers 1998 and Campbell 2009: abstracts only. The mean shoulder-centre position relative to the acromion and Campbell's offset values are unknown.
- Rab 2002: abstract only. Its constant-offset ratio is unverified.

**Not reachable**
- Clauser 1969, Chandler 1975 and McConville 1980 (DTIC: "The request is blocked").
- Dempster 1955 (Deep Blue: Cloudflare challenge).
- The Wayback Machine (connection reset).
- So no cadaver or stereophotogrammetric segment breadth/depth tables were obtained.

**No data found**
- Upper arm and neck: no source gives breadth and depth at the same level. The upper arm's aspect (about 0.55–0.7) is indirect, from Heymsfield 1982 (CT, muscle compartment only, abstract) and Liu 2018 (photo errors). Neither says which view is wider. The neck at the Adam's apple has no shape data at all.
- Shoulder joint centre, side to side: no source gives its position relative to the acromion. De Leva assumes joint centres lie on segment axes.

**Limits of the sources used**
- De Leva's offsets come from six cadavers (Chandler), scaled to Zatsiorsky's subjects, with no SD.
- AIST covers Japanese men aged 18–29 (1991), and only means are public, so its limb ratios are ratios of means. Hypertrophied limbs may differ.
- ANSUR II has no limb breadths or depths, no crown-to-chin height and no iliospinale height.
- The ANSUR head height (0.129 of stature) is scaled with a Japanese ratio. The inter-hip distance (169–188 mm) is an estimate built from assumed inputs.
- Hu 2022 (hip centre vs trochanter) is a small elderly fracture sample, and the direction of its 6 mm distance is not stated.
- The chest factor of 1.24 applies to ANSUR's squeezed caliper breadth. No dataset gives a photo-outline chest width with lats to test the ellipse against.
- ANSUR II is soldiers, not bodybuilders. Every ratio applied to enhanced or comic builds is an extrapolation."
}

2. "The scale" plate, which is the hero. A widened template man (ANSUR II proportions, grey, dotted, labelled NOT A BUILD) stands at 24, 48, 96, 192 and 384, then the meatball circle at 924. 6. "Known limits", in short bullet form.

Rex and Ollie are real traces from the turnarounds. My mock-grade tracer uses a saturation/dark/warm mask, hole fill, Moore boundary tracing and Ramer-Douglas-Peucker simplification.   "axis": "The axis is log, not broken. A broken axis would cut out exactly the empty stretches (about 40–50, 84–150, 190–924) that the brief wants visibly empty.

Hero ruler (slide rule):
- Ticks every 1 from 15–50, every 5 from 55–100, every 10 from 110–200, and every 50 from 250–1,000.
- Four tick lengths: 5, 9, 14, 20 px. Decade marks at 100 and 1,000 are tallest, with bold numerals.
- Desktop labels: 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 80, 100, 150, 200, 300, 500, 1,000. Phone: 15, 20, 30, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1,000.
- Axis title: "SCORE (FFMI AT 1.80 M, KG/M²)".
- The bottom edge carries a conversion scale, not a second axis: kg of fat-free mass for a 1.80 m man (S × 3.24), labelled 50 kg, 100, 200, 500, 1t, 2t, 3t. It is one quantity in two units, like °C and °F.

Ranking track:
- Percentage-positioned on the same log mapping, so it needs no resize maths.
- Hairline gridlines at 20/30/50/100(darker)/200/500, plus a faint red rule at the extrapolation boundary.

Ranges:
- Each range is a bar from S at high fat to S at low fat, 8 px tall, with 1.5 px ink end caps 15 px tall and an ink diamond at the working value.
- Hatched bar (group-colour diagonal stripes) = body fat assumed (estimate). Solid bar = body fat measured (score status derived).

Sticky axis and zoom:
- The ranking's axis header is sticky (top: env(safe-area-inset-top)). It shows the void hatching and "beyond measured humans: extrapolated →".
- The option "Zoom 15 to 50" re-maps the same log scale over 15–50. Off-scale rows then read "off scale: 151–168 →" at the right edge.",
  "gaps_and_limits": "Empty stretches:
- Computed from the data: stretches of the scale that no build's full range covers, when the gap ratio is above 1.2. The top gap always runs to 924.
- Hero: drawn as diagonal hatching (--void) through the lanes below the ruler, labelled on desktop "NO BUILD" and "NO BUILD · 189–924", and listed in words in the notes ("No build lands between 42 and 57, between 90 and 151, or anywhere above 189...").
- Sticky axis: shown as the same hatching.
- Ranking: inserted in score order as gap rows, e.g. "NOTHING FROM 42 TO 57", with a bordered hatched block on the track and "Empty until Step 2".
- Lane ranges are drawn per build, never as a group span, so no lane appears to bridge a void.

Natural-limit anchors:
- Kouri 25 is an ink hairline through all lanes, labelled "Kouri 25: top of 74 drug-free men". The limits section adds "a sample maximum, not a ceiling".
- Frame-based predictions are an ink bracket under the lanes: "Frame-based natural-limit predictions (Butt): 25–28 · weak evidence · mock". Its evidence grade is part of the label.

End of human data:
- A red rule at the highest measured human (mock 40), labelled "Measured humans end · beyond here every score is an extrapolation →".
- Every row past it gets an "extrapolated" chip.

Functional limits:
- Three dashed alarm-red brackets sit between the template figures and the ruler: T (thighs touch to the knee), A (arms can no longer hang), F (hands can no longer reach the face).
- Each is drawn as a band, not a line, because its position depends on the template's widening rule and on the definition.
- Labelled "placeholder" on desktop and "T ?" on phone, with a chip "POSITIONS NOT YET COMPUTED".
- In the build, each band comes from the template geometry: the widened figures are the evidence, and the band edges mark where each condition first and fully fails.

The meatball:
- A neutral-grey circle the full figure height, at 924, labelled "924 MEATBALL".
- A heavy ink rule at 924 through the lanes, with 924–1,000 shaded and labelled "past 924: impossible".
- In the ranking, a meatball row: "A solid ball of muscle as tall as the figure.", score 924, chip DERIVED, note "Nothing can score higher."",
  "marking_key": "The outline is drawn per body part (head, neck, chest, waist, upper arm, forearm with hand, thigh, calf with foot), so the marking can change along one figure. Coleman, for example, has a solid chest, waist, arm and calf with a dotted forearm, neck and head.
- Solid ink: the part comes from this build's own girth with status measured, reported or official.
- Dotted ink (round-cap dots): the template fills the part in, scaled by weight. This covers unknown and derived girths, and the head always.
- Dash-dot in --duo-edge gold: traced from art.

This is a deliberate change from the task's example (dashed = template, dotted = art). The house chips already use dashed = reported and dotted = derived, so I made dotted mean template-derived (matching the chip meaning) and gave art a third pattern. It needs the owner's agreement.

Tails:
- Drawn but not filled: group-colour hatching with a grey dashed edge.
- Key text: "Hatched: drawn but left out of the score (tails)".
- Rex's tail shows between his legs in the front view. Ollie's is hidden in the front view and appears in the side view.

Crest and horns rise above a grey skull-top datum line drawn through every figure cell. Key: "Grey line: top of the skull, the height the score uses. Crests and horns rise above it."

Overstated comics:
- The Thing (rock) and Colossus in armoured form (steel) get a red dotted arrow pointing left from the bar ("Arrow left: part of the weight isn't muscle (rock, steel). The true score is lower.") plus a red note in the row.
- Thor gets a red note ("Asgardian tissue is said to be denser than human. The score may be overstated.").
- Wolverine sits after the meatball with no bar, a "not scored" track label, a "—" reading and the note "Not scored: his adamantium skeleton adds unknown weight."

Every number in a row (height, weight, fat range, girths) sits inside a box with its status border, using the same vocabulary as the chips. The score carries a word chip (ESTIMATE or DERIVED), plus EXTRAPOLATED when it applies.",

  "copy": "Mock ribbon: "Design mockup · every number on this page is a placeholder · not for review of facts".

Masthead:
- Eyebrow: "Men's builds · muscle level, height taken out"
- H1: "Build Comparison"
- Verdict: "Ordinary men score 20 to 26. The most muscular people measured reach about 38. Rex and Ollie score about 160 and 180. No body can score above 924: that is a solid ball of muscle."
- Spec line: "49 builds · men only · score = 1.8 × fat-free mass ÷ height³ · log scale · [MOCK NUMBERS]"

The scale:
- H2: "One ruler for every build"
- Verdict: "Equal steps on this ruler are equal ratios: 20 to 40 is the same distance as 100 to 200."
- Sub: "Top: the average soldier's shape, widened step by step, drawn from ANSUR II proportions. It is a template, not a build. Below the ruler: every build, one tick each, by group. Hatched stretches hold no build at all."
- Figure caption: "TEMPLATE MAN, WIDENED · NOT A BUILD"
- Notes:
  - "EMPTY STRETCHES: No build lands between 42 and 57, between 90 and 151, or anywhere above 189. These stretches stay empty until figures measured from art fill them (Step 2)."
  - "T · A · F: Where the body stops working, found by widening the template: T thighs touch all the way to the knee, A arms can no longer hang by the sides, F hands can no longer reach the face. [POSITIONS NOT YET COMPUTED]"
  - "THE TWO SCALES: The ruler's top edge is the score. Its bottom edge is the same reading as fat-free mass (everything except fat) for a man 1.80 m tall."

Key:
- H2: "Key"
- Verdict: "The outline says where a shape came from. The box around a number says how sure it is."
- Outline entries: "Solid: drawn from this build's own girth." / "Dotted: no girth for this part, so the template fills it in, scaled by weight." / "Dash-dot: traced from art." / "Hatched: drawn but left out of the score (tails)." / "Grey line: top of the skull, the height the score uses. Crests and horns rise above it."
- Bar entries: "Hatched bar: body fat assumed. The ends are the low and high guess; the diamond is the working value." / "Solid bar: body fat measured. The ends are its stated spread." / "Arrow left: part of the weight isn't muscle (rock, steel). The true score is lower." / "Hatched band: no build lands here."
- Status entries: "measured: Taken with a tape, scale or scanner, or a statistic of such measurements." / "official: Printed by the publisher, or an official sport record." / "reported: Stated by a magazine, the athlete or a fan site. Nobody checked it." / "derived: Calculated from other numbers." / "estimate: Assumed or modelled, with a stated range."

Ranking:
- H2: "Every build, lowest to highest"
- Verdict: "Each bar spans the score across plausible body fat. Bars that overlap can't be ranked against each other."
- Sub: "Body fat is known for only a few builds, so most bars are hatched: their width is an assumption. Plain FFMI (fat-free mass ÷ height², kg/m²) sits under each score so you can compare it with the familiar scale."
- Gap row: "Nothing from 42 to 57" / "Empty until Step 2"

How the score works:
- H2: "FFMI for the same body at 1.80 m"
- Verdict: "Shrink or stretch every body to 1.80 m without changing its shape, then take its FFMI. That is the score."
- Body text: "FFMI is fat-free mass divided by height squared. It is fair between people of similar height. It is not fair between a 1.8 m man and a 3 m dinosaur: scale a body up at the same shape and its mass grows with height cubed, so its FFMI keeps rising even though it is no more muscular. Dividing by height cubed fixes that. Multiplying by 1.8 puts the result in FFMI units for a man 1.80 m tall, so ordinary readings stay familiar."
- Note: "Height is to the top of the skull. Rex's crest and Ollie's horns don't count; nor do their tails. Every 1% of height moves the score about 3%."

Bench:
- H2: "Measure a model sheet"
- Verdict: "Upload one sheet with front, side and back views. You get the volume, mass, girths and score, and how far to trust each."

Target outline:
- H2: "Draw an outline for any score"
- Verdict: "Pick a score and a base shape. You get front and side outlines at the model-sheet spec, to use as control images."

Limits:
- H2: "What this chart can't tell you"
- Verdict: "It measures how much muscle a body carries for its height. It says nothing about strength, health or how a body moves."",

2. **The widened template reads as fat.** Uniform widening grows the waist and hips and looks obese, not muscular. The mock uses a "waist grows least" pattern with made-up exponents (WIDEN_E). 3. **Functional limits need definitions before geometry.** For example, "arms can't hang" could mean the arm angle needed to clear the torso goes above X°. The results also depend on fixed skeletal joints (the mock assumes the shoulder and hip joints don't move). Expect bands, not lines.

5. **Gaps depend on the gap rule and the fat ranges.** Wide assumed ranges (Kingpin 10–35%) can close the 39–50 gap. The build must fix one rule, either full ranges or working values plus a minimum ratio, and state it.

THE LINEUP
Verdict: "Everyone stands at the same height, in score order. Only the build differs."
Sub-line: "Each figure stands on its score. The spacing is not to scale; the tape below is. Empty floor means no build has been measured there yet. Tap a figure for its sources."
Gap plates: "39–50 / Empty. No build measured here yet." and "189–924 / Empty. Nothing measured between Ollie and the meatball."
Post: "KOURI 25 · SAMPLE TOP"
Meatball plate: "924 / The meatball / end of the scale"
Duo plates: "tail not counted"
Flags: "▲ rock, not muscle", "▲ denser tissue claimed"

Drawer facts: "Range across 5–10% body fat, which is assumed." and "The same as the score, because he is 1.80 m tall."

HOW TO READ A FIGURE
Verdict: "Every figure is a flat shape. Its edge says where the shape came from."
Key entries:
- "Solid: from a tape measure. A measured, official or reported girth."
- "Dashed: filled in from the template. No girth for this part, so the Army median's shape is scaled to the weight."

- "Hatched: not counted. Rex's and Ollie's tails stay out of the score."
- "Skull-top line. All figures are drawn to it. Rex's crest and Ollie's horns rise above it."

TO SCALE
Verdict: "Real men sit between about 20 and 38. Past that there is fiction, the duo, and empty floor."

Legend: "body-fat range, middle value" · "overstated: not all of it is muscle" · "empty: no build measured yet"

  "risks": "1. **Rank order is not to scale.** A ranked lineup shows order, not distance. A critic may read the spacing as distance. Mitigations: the sub-line ("The spacing is not to scale; the tape below is"), numbers on every plate, and the to-scale strip directly below. Gap tiles are log-proportional with a minimum width, which is a hint only. It might be cleaner to make all gap tiles equal and let only the strip carry proportion.
2. **The meatball is not a hard maximum.** It is a chosen end of scale. A body as wide as it is tall (a cylinder) holds π/4 H³ against π/6 H³ for a ball, so it scores about 1.5× more (about 1,390). The page must say "the scale ends at 924" and give the owner's reason. Never write "no body can pass 924". The brief's sentence "A figure can't hold more volume than a ball as tall as itself" is wrong as written and should be raised with the owner.
3. **Edge styles blur on phones.** At H = 92, dotted and dashed edges are hard to tell apart, and per-region marking on small figures is subtle at any size. The drawer (H = 230) is where the marking is readable. Consider thicker strokes on phones, or a "show marking" emphasis on the selected figure only.
4. **The palette breaks two validator rules on purpose.** The everyday slate fails the chroma floor, the umber fails the lightness band, and gold is about 1.7:1 against the wall. The design relies on ink edges plus direct labels. CVD and normal-vision separation pass for all pairs in both themes.
5. **Page length.** The phone lineup is about 1,350 px for the key 20 and would be about 3,000 px for all 49. Desktop is three rows. Default to "Key 20" and state the selection rule, or "key" reads as cherry-picking.
6. **The tail is hard to read in front view.** Rex's front-view tail is only a small bulb between the legs and reads as a ball. The side view shows it properly. The plates' "tail not counted" carries it in the front view.
7. **Skull-top lines are eyeballed.** The mock used Rex at y = 45 and Ollie at y = 42 on the turnarounds, crop coordinates. The build must use the brief's duo.jpg measurement (3.858 mm/px), labelled "measured from art, estimate".
8. **The trace is mock quality.** It used a saturation-or-dark mask, a 2–3 px blur and RDP at 1.6 px. Rex's spines and glints add noise, and Ollie's horn tips are slightly trimmed by the blur. Reusable as a start: trace.py and traces-norm.json.
9. **The arm rule decides the first limit.** The mock's arm-angle rule (the smallest angle that clears the torso, from 16°) also decides the "arms can't hang" limit. The build must define and source that rule before any position is shown. The limits section must keep the "not worked out" wording until it is.
10. **Plain FFMI for the duo needs a gloss.** At real height their plain FFMI is about 250–300 and may confuse readers. The plate should explain why it is so much higher than the score.
11. **SVG patterns use CSS variables.** Patterns and fills use var() in presentation attributes. That works in Chromium, but Safari should be checked.
12. **The sample sheet is too heavy as-is.** The 2.2 MB turnaround PNG would bloat the page and needs re-encoding before it is inlined.

  "risks": "1. **Crowding at full scale.** About 40 human and human-sized builds fall in 15–40, the left ~23% of the track. Their bars are 10–20 px, and on a phone they shrink to little more than the diamond and caps. The "Zoom 15 to 50" option makes them readable (see 1280-modes.png). The owner should pick the default; the brief favours one honest full scale.

2. **The widened template reads as fat.** Uniform widening grows the waist and hips and looks obese, not muscular. The mock uses a "waist grows least" pattern with made-up exponents (WIDEN_E). The build needs a sourced widening rule, for example girth-versus-FFMI regressions in ANSUR II or bodybuilders' girth ratios. That rule also moves where T, A and F land.

3. **Functional limits need definitions before geometry.** For example, "arms can't hang" could mean the arm angle needed to clear the torso goes above X°. The results also depend on fixed skeletal joints (the mock assumes the shoulder and hip joints don't move). Expect bands, not lines.

4. **Outline coding differs from the task's example.** The mock uses solid = own girth, dotted = template, dash-dot = art, chosen so it doesn't clash with the house chips (dashed = reported, dotted = derived). This needs sign-off. The dots and the dash-dot are distinguishable at row size (52–84 px), but only just; the 210 px detail figure is clear.

5. **Gaps depend on the gap rule and the fat ranges.** Wide assumed ranges (Kingpin 10–35%) can close the 39–50 gap. The build must fix one rule, either full ranges or working values plus a minimum ratio, and state it.

6. **Palette compromises.**
   - Everyday grey (chroma) and duo umber (lightness) deliberately fail the validator bands.
   - Gold and grey are below 3:1 contrast against the plate; ink outlines and text labels carry them.
   - Dark-mode CVD separation is 7.4, legal only because every row has text.
   - The duo's dark-mode tick (#7A5438) is dim in the hero lanes.

7. **Tracing is mock grade.** The tail polygons were placed by hand: Rex's tail overlaps his legs in the front view, a known art defect. The skull-top pixel rows were eyeballed (Rex at 42/40, Ollie at 38/36), and the back view in the bench is a mirrored front. These are fine for a design mock, but not for Step 1 numbers.

8. **Saving images is unverified.** It relies on right-click or long-press saving an image inside the artifact sandbox. If that fails, the fallback is copying the image's data URL with the copy button.

9. **Page length.** About 14,800 px on a phone and 10,100 px on desktop. Group filters and the name-to-detail toggle help; a compact density option may be wanted.

10. **Placeholders and cascade risk.** The extrapolation boundary (40), the frame-based bracket (25–28), the T/A/F positions and every score are placeholders. One cascade bug was already found and fixed: a .foot class collided between the row foot and the page footer. The build should namespace its classes.

  "axis": "Log scale, not a broken axis.

  "marking_key": "**How figures are built.** Each figure is drawn as region pieces: head, neck, chest, waist/hip, upper arm, forearm+hand, thigh, calf+foot. Strokes go under the fills at twice their width, so only the outer half shows and region seams vanish. Each region gets its own edge style:
- **Solid:** "from a tape measure". A measured, official or reported girth.
- **Dashed (6/4):** "filled in from the template". The Army median's shape scaled to the weight.
- **Dotted (0.1/4.2 round caps, about 2.9 px):** "measured from art". Rex and Ollie, traced from their turnarounds.

The marking varies along one figure. Coleman shows solid chest, waist, arm and calf, and dashed thigh, forearm and neck. The drawer caption says so in words, and the drawer's facts row names each part with its chip (reported / derived / template).

**Tails.** The visible tail region is clipped to the silhouette and filled with a hatch of duo-colour lines over the wall colour, with a dashed duo outline. It reads as a hole that is not counted. Rex's front view shows only the bulb between his legs; the side view shows the whole tail hatched. Ollie's tail is hidden in the front view, so the plate line "tail not counted" carries it. The key reads: "Hatched: not counted. Rex's and Ollie's tails stay out of the score."

**Crest and horns.** Rex's crest and Ollie's horns rise above the dashed skull-top line shared by every figure.

**Overstated comics.**

  "copy": "Masthead (on the yellow log tape band):
H1: "BUILD COMPARISON"
Lede: "Drawn at one height, an ordinary man scores about 24. The biggest pros reach about 38 and comic giants about 80. Rex and Ollie score about 160 and 180. The scale ends at 924, the score of a solid ball of muscle as tall as the figure." [chip: all estimates]
Spec: "49 men · score = muscle carried if the body were 1.80 m tall · every number says what it is"

Controls: "Heights: Same height | Real heights", "View: Front | Side", "Builds: Key 20 | All 49".

THE LINEUP
Verdict: "Everyone stands at the same height, in score order. Only the build differs."
Sub-line: "Each figure stands on its score. The spacing is not to scale; the tape below is. Empty floor means no build has been measured there yet. Tap a figure for its sources."
Gap plates: "39–50 / Empty. No build measured here yet." and "189–924 / Empty. Nothing measured between Ollie and the meatball."
Post: "KOURI 25 · SAMPLE TOP"
Meatball plate: "924 / The meatball / end of the scale"
Duo plates: "tail not counted"
Flags: "▲ rock, not muscle", "▲ denser tissue claimed"
Drawer caption: "Solid edge: chest, waist, flexed arm and calf from his reported girths. Dashed: thigh, forearm and neck filled in from the template."
Drawer facts: "Range across 5–10% body fat, which is assumed." and "The same as the score, because he is 1.80 m tall."

HOW TO READ A FIGURE
Verdict: "Every figure is a flat shape. Its edge says where the shape came from."
Key entries:
- "Solid: from a tape measure. A measured, official or reported girth."
- "Dashed: filled in from the template. No girth for this part, so the Army median's shape is scaled to the weight."
- "Dotted: measured from art. Rex and Ollie, traced from their turnarounds."
- "Hatched: not counted. Rex's and Ollie's tails stay out of the score."
- "Skull-top line. All figures are drawn to it. Rex's crest and Ollie's horns rise above it."
- "Plate: the score range, the name, then plain FFMI. Both carry the chip's status. EST: estimate (body fat assumed). DER: derived (body fat measured). ART: measured from art."
- "Overstated. Part of the weight is not muscle (rock, steel), or the tissue is claimed denser."

TO SCALE
Verdict: "Real men sit between about 20 and 38. Past that there is fiction, the duo, and empty floor."
Sub-line: "A log tape: each step to the right multiplies the score. Each bar runs across the plausible body fat for that build; the dot is the middle value."
Bracket: "three body limits fall somewhere in 40–200 (not yet worked out)"
Legend: "body-fat range, middle value" · "overstated: not all of it is muscle" · "empty: no build measured yet"

WHERE THE BODY STOPS WORKING
Verdict: "Three limits come from the drawn body itself. Where they fall is not worked out yet."
Sub-line: "The page widens the average man's outline until each thing happens, then reads off the score."
Plates:
- "Arms can't hang down / The arm meets the torso before it reaches the side."
- "Thighs touch to the knee / No daylight between the legs above the knee."
- "Hands can't reach the face / Upper arm and forearm too thick to fold that far."

THE SCORE AND THE NATURAL LIMIT
Verdict: "The score asks how much muscle a body would carry at 1.80 m tall. No hard natural ceiling is known."
Formula: "score = 1.8 × fat-free mass ÷ height³"
Explanation: "Fat-free mass is everything but fat: muscle, bone, organs, water. Scale a body up at the same shape and its mass grows with height cubed, so dividing by height cubed takes size out. The result equals plain FFMI (fat-free mass ÷ height²) for a man who is 1.80 m tall."
Kouri: "Kouri 1995. The highest of 74 men who said they never used steroids. A sample's top, not a ceiling."

MEASURE A CHARACTER
Verdict: "Load an A-pose model sheet, type the height and density, and get a build you can add."
Sub-line: "The sheet needs front, side and back views at one scale. Results stay on this page: copy them, or screenshot the outlines. Downloads are blocked here."",

  "risks": "1. **Rank order is not to scale.** A ranked lineup shows order, not distance. A critic may read the spacing as distance. Mitigations: the sub-line ("The spacing is not to scale; the tape below is"), numbers on every plate, and the to-scale strip directly below. Gap tiles are log-proportional with a minimum width, which is a hint only. It might be cleaner to make all gap tiles equal and let only the strip carry proportion.
2. **The meatball is not a hard maximum.** It is a chosen end of scale. A body as wide as it is tall (a cylinder) holds π/4 H³ against π/6 H³ for a ball, so it scores about 1.5× more (about 1,390). The page must say "the scale ends at 924" and give the owner's reason. Never write "no body can pass 924". The brief's sentence "A figure can't hold more volume than a ball as tall as itself" is wrong as written and should be raised with the owner.
3. **Edge styles blur on phones.** At H = 92, dotted and dashed edges are hard to tell apart, and per-region marking on small figures is subtle at any size. The drawer (H = 230) is where the marking is readable. Consider thicker strokes on phones, or a "show marking" emphasis on the selected figure only.
4. **The palette breaks two validator rules on purpose.** The everyday slate fails the chroma floor, the umber fails the lightness band, and gold is about 1.7:1 against the wall. The design relies on ink edges plus direct labels. CVD and normal-vision separation pass for all pairs in both themes.
5. **Page length.** The phone lineup is about 1,350 px for the key 20 and would be about 3,000 px for all 49. Desktop is three rows. Default to "Key 20" and state the selection rule, or "key" reads as cherry-picking.
6. **The tail is hard to read in front view.** Rex's front-view tail is only a small bulb between the legs and reads as a ball. The side view shows it properly. The plates' "tail not counted" carries it in the front view.
7. **Skull-top lines are eyeballed.** The mock used Rex at y = 45 and Ollie at y = 42 on the turnarounds, crop coordinates. The build must use the brief's duo.jpg measurement (3.858 mm/px), labelled "measured from art, estimate".
8. **The trace is mock quality.** It used a saturation-or-dark mask, a 2–3 px blur and RDP at 1.6 px. Rex's spines and glints add noise, and Ollie's horn tips are slightly trimmed by the blur. Reusable as a start: trace.py and traces-norm.json.
9. **The arm rule decides the first limit.** The mock's arm-angle rule (the smallest angle that clears the torso, from 16°) also decides the "arms can't hang" limit. The build must define and source that rule before any position is shown. The limits section must keep the "not worked out" wording until it is.
10. **Plain FFMI for the duo needs a gloss.** At real height their plain FFMI is about 250–300 and may confuse readers. The plate should explain why it is so much higher than the score.
11. **SVG patterns use CSS variables.** Patterns and fills use var() in presentation attributes. That works in Chromium, but Safari should be checked.
12. **The sample sheet is too heavy as-is.** The 2.2 MB turnaround PNG would bloat the page and needs re-encoding before it is inlined.
13. **Every number in the mock is a placeholder.** All are marked with purple MOCK chips or the mock banner. None are research values."

10. The sticky rail depends on 100svh inside the claude.ai frame. It falls back to min-height 520 and max 900. Check it in the published frame.

11. Tool:
- The mock's landmark line positions on duo.jpg are eyeballed.

13. Dark mode. The pale chalk fill of the geometry figures is low-contrast against the wall; the chalk outline carries it.

14. Fonts and tokens are reused from the sister page on purpose, for family. A reviewer wanting a distinct identity for this page should be pointed to styles.html."

You are designing one page: "Build Comparison", a new self-contained HTML page (claude.ai Artifact) in /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-comparison/. Read /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-comparison/BRIEF.md and /home/user/rex-strength-lab/CLAUDE.md first. Look at the art: /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-comparison/assets/rex-turnaround.png and ollie-turnaround.png (A-pose turnarounds, the style key), /home/user/rex-strength-lab/rex-strength-lab/assets/duo.jpg. Look at the sister page's design system in /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-calculator/src/app.html (a tailor's measurement sheet: tokens --paper/--sheet/--ink/--tape/--chalk, fonts Big Shoulders Display, Public Sans, IBM Plex Mono) and the screenshots in /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-calculator/shots/ if present (run node /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-calculator/test/shots.js to make them if absent; it writes to /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-calculator/shots/, which is git-ignored).
What the page does: it ranks MEN's builds by a size-independent "muscle level" score S = 1.8 x fat-free mass / height^3 (FFMI after rescaling the body to 1.80 m at the same shape), shown beside plain FFMI. Scale runs from about 15 to 1,000 (log or broken axis). Builds (about 49 men): ANSUR II soldiers (5th/50th/95th percentile, plus 3 subgroups), NHANES US men, natural athletes (Kouri non-users, Chappell natural pros, Mr America 1938-54 mean, Steve Reeves), 12 bodybuilders (Coleman, Arnold, Yates, Cutler, Heath, Big Ramy, Oliva, 5 study groups), 5 strongmen/lifters (Shaw, Bjornsson, Hall, Talakhadze, Kraemer group), about 20 male comic characters (Superman to Darkseid, Hulks, Juggernaut, the Thing, Colossus), and Rex and Ollie (3 m original characters, measured from art). Rough scores at assumed body fat: everyday 22-26; natural athletes 22-25; bodybuilders 24-35; strongmen 32-38; comics 16-81 (Thor/Thing 57, Darkseid/Hulks 66-81); Rex about 160 and Ollie about 180 (height to the top of the skull, tail excluded, 7.5% fat). Each score is a RANGE across plausible body fat (most body fat is unknown) and must be shown as a range. Gaps with no anchors must stay visibly empty: about 39-50, about 81-140, and above Ollie up to the "meatball" (a solid ball of muscle as tall as the figure, about 924, the top of the scale). Three functional limits are marked by geometry on a drawn human template whose widths are scaled up: arms can no longer hang by the sides; thighs touch all the way to the knee; hands can no longer reach the face (rough guesses: somewhere between 40 and 200; treat their positions as unknown placeholders). Natural-limit anchors also need marking (Kouri's FFMI 25 is a sample maximum, not a ceiling; frame-based predictions). Some comic scores are overstated or not comparable (the Thing is rock; Colossus armoured is steel; Thor's Asgardian tissue is claimed denser; Wolverine has adamantium, excluded).
Silhouettes: flat filled shapes for every build, all at the same drawn height by default (option: real heights side by side; option: side view). Builds differ only in their outline marking: measured (solid edge), derived from a template build (dashed edge), measured from art (dotted edge), explained in a key; markings can vary along one figure (e.g. measured chest, template forearm). Human figures are drawn from data (ANSUR II proportions), never from the duo's shapes; Rex and Ollie are traced from their turnarounds (their crest/horns rise above the common skull-top line; their tails are excluded from the score and should read as excluded).   "risks": "1. **Crowding at full scale.** About 40 human and human-sized builds fall in 15–40, the left ~23% of the track. Their bars are 10–20 px, and on a phone they shrink to little more than the diamond and caps. The "Zoom 15 to 50" option makes them readable (see 1280-modes.png). The owner should pick the default; the brief favours one honest full scale.

2. **The widened template reads as fat.** Uniform widening grows the waist and hips and looks obese, not muscular. The mock uses a "waist grows least" pattern with made-up exponents (WIDEN_E). The build needs a sourced widening rule, for example girth-versus-FFMI regressions in ANSUR II or bodybuilders' girth ratios. That rule also moves where T, A and F land.

3. **Functional limits need definitions before geometry.** For example, "arms can't hang" could mean the arm angle needed to clear the torso goes above X°. The results also depend on fixed skeletal joints (the mock assumes the shoulder and hip joints don't move). Expect bands, not lines.

4. **Outline coding differs from the task's example.** The mock uses solid = own girth, dotted = template, dash-dot = art, chosen so it doesn't clash with the house chips (dashed = reported, dotted = derived). This needs sign-off. The dots and the dash-dot are distinguishable at row size (52–84 px), but only just; the 210 px detail figure is clear.

5. **Gaps depend on the gap rule and the fat ranges.** Wide assumed ranges (Kingpin 10–35%) can close the 39–50 gap. The build must fix one rule, either full ranges or working values plus a minimum ratio, and state it.

6. **Palette compromises.**
   - Everyday grey (chroma) and duo umber (lightness) deliberately fail the validator bands.
   - Gold and grey are below 3:1 contrast against the plate; ink outlines and text labels carry them.
   - Dark-mode CVD separation is 7.4, legal only because every row has text.
   - The duo's dark-mode tick (#7A5438) is dim in the hero lanes.

7. **Tracing is mock grade.** The tail polygons were placed by hand: Rex's tail overlaps his legs in the front view, a known art defect. The skull-top pixel rows were eyeballed (Rex at 42/40, Ollie at 38/36), and the back view in the bench is a mirrored front. These are fine for a design mock, but not for Step 1 numbers.

8. **Saving images is unverified.** It relies on right-click or long-press saving an image inside the artifact sandbox. If that fails, the fallback is copying the image's data URL with the copy button.

9. **Page length.** About 14,800 px on a phone and 10,100 px on desktop. Group filters and the name-to-detail toggle help; a compact density option may be wanted.

10. **Placeholders and cascade risk.** The extrapolation boundary (40), the frame-based bracket (25–28), the T/A/F positions and every score are placeholders. One cascade bug was already found and fixed: a .foot class collided between the row foot and the page footer. The build should namespace its classes.

11. **Real heights in rows.** Humans become about 45 px tall, which is too small to compare. A dedicated real-height lineup strip, or doing it in the detail view, may serve better."

  "risks": "1. **Rank order is not to scale.** A ranked lineup shows order, not distance. A critic may read the spacing as distance. Mitigations: the sub-line ("The spacing is not to scale; the tape below is"), numbers on every plate, and the to-scale strip directly below. Gap tiles are log-proportional with a minimum width, which is a hint only. It might be cleaner to make all gap tiles equal and let only the strip carry proportion.
2. **The meatball is not a hard maximum.** It is a chosen end of scale. A body as wide as it is tall (a cylinder) holds π/4 H³ against π/6 H³ for a ball, so it scores about 1.5× more (about 1,390). The page must say "the scale ends at 924" and give the owner's reason. Never write "no body can pass 924". The brief's sentence "A figure can't hold more volume than a ball as tall as itself" is wrong as written and should be raised with the owner.
3. **Edge styles blur on phones.** At H = 92, dotted and dashed edges are hard to tell apart, and per-region marking on small figures is subtle at any size. The drawer (H = 230) is where the marking is readable. Consider thicker strokes on phones, or a "show marking" emphasis on the selected figure only.
4. **The palette breaks two validator rules on purpose.** The everyday slate fails the chroma floor, the umber fails the lightness band, and gold is about 1.7:1 against the wall. The design relies on ink edges plus direct labels. CVD and normal-vision separation pass for all pairs in both themes.
5. **Page length.** The phone lineup is about 1,350 px for the key 20 and would be about 3,000 px for all 49. Desktop is three rows. Default to "Key 20" and state the selection rule, or "key" reads as cherry-picking.
6. **The tail is hard to read in front view.** Rex's front-view tail is only a small bulb between the legs and reads as a ball. The side view shows it properly. The plates' "tail not counted" carries it in the front view.
7. **Skull-top lines are eyeballed.** The mock used Rex at y = 45 and Ollie at y = 42 on the turnarounds, crop coordinates. The build must use the brief's duo.jpg measurement (3.858 mm/px), labelled "measured from art, estimate".
8. **The trace is mock quality.** It used a saturation-or-dark mask, a 2–3 px blur and RDP at 1.6 px. Rex's spines and glints add noise, and Ollie's horn tips are slightly trimmed by the blur. Reusable as a start: trace.py and traces-norm.json.
9. **The arm rule decides the first limit.** The mock's arm-angle rule (the smallest angle that clears the torso, from 16°) also decides the "arms can't hang" limit. The build must define and source that rule before any position is shown. The limits section must keep the "not worked out" wording until it is.
10. **Plain FFMI for the duo needs a gloss.** At real height their plain FFMI is about 250–300 and may confuse readers. The plate should explain why it is so much higher than the score.
11. **SVG patterns use CSS variables.** Patterns and fills use var() in presentation attributes. That works in Chromium, but Safari should be checked.
12. **The sample sheet is too heavy as-is.** The 2.2 MB turnaround PNG would bloat the page and needs re-encoding before it is inlined.
13. **Every number in the mock is a placeholder.** All are marked with purple MOCK chips or the mock banner. None are research values."

3. The drawer at H=230, with a caption that says in words which parts are solid and which are dashed. This is where the per-part marking can actually be read on a phone.
4. It calls 924 a chosen end ('The scale ends at 924') and gives the cylinder argument. That is honest.
5. Wall rules at ANSUR landmark heights (skull, waist, knee) behind every figure. With them, same-height figures read as comparable.
6. The limits strip of four template figures, with the deciding body part outlined in chalk blue. It shows each functional limit as a picture, not a bracket.",
    "problems": "1. The mock's controls do nothing. Clicking 'Real heights', 'All 49' or 'Side' at 390 px leaves the page height (8,075 px) and its markup unchanged. The 49-build phone lineup (their own estimate is about 3,000 px) and the side and real-height modes are unproven.
2. 'Key 20' is the default, so 29 builds are hidden on arrival. To a critic this reads as cherry-picking unless the selection rule sits right beside the toggle, and the mock does not show that rule.
3. The full-bleed log tape at the top has no builds on it and sits directly above a lineup that is not to scale. That invites the reader to read figure positions against the tape. The sub-line saying 'not to scale' is 12 px grey text.
4. Plate type is small on the phone: names 11 px, 'FFMI x–y' 9.5 px, and the overstated flags ('▲ DENSER TISSUE CLAIMED') 9.5 px in red capitals. The status chips are 8.5 px abbreviations (EST/DER/ART), so the reader has to look them up in the key.
5. Bench sheet guide labels render at 4.1 px, which is unreadable. The tool's 'HEIGHT' field defaults to 3.048 m, which is crest height. That contradicts the canon that scores use height to the top of the skull.
6. On the phone, the 81–140 gap tile is narrower than one figure cell. It reads as a small gap even though it is as large as everyday-to-Coleman.
7. The limit figures use '≈ 60 / ≈ 95 / ≈ 150', which look like findings despite their MOCK chips. The widened template looks obese."
   },
   {
    "angle": "Phone-first scroll tape with stops and a pinned to-scale rail",
    "accuracy_honesty": 8,
    "readability": 8,
    "phone": 8,
    "distinctiveness": 7,
    "feasibility": 7,
    "best_ideas": "1. Every stop opens with a yellow score tag ('SCORE 41 TO 57'), a display headline and a one-line verdict ('Nothing measured scores 41 to 57. No human and no comic character.'). That is the right shape for an ADHD reader.
2. It has the most legible phone type of the three. Plate scores are 17 px, chips use full words (ESTIMATE, DERIVED), and FFMI and the overstated notes are 11–11.5 px. Only the rail numbers (9.5 px) and the bench sheet labels (7.8 px) fall below 11 px.
3. A sticky to-scale rail with a current-stop box. While scrolling at Rex's stop it shows the box sitting at 150–190 on the log tape (v-reader-dpr2.png). Proportion stays visible while the figures get room.
4. Gap edges and comparison sentences are computed, not typed ('as big as from an ordinary man to Ronnie Coleman', 'about twice the Hulk').
5. The meatball stop calls 924 'a chosen end point, not a law of geometry' and shows the formula. The natural-limit stop has status-chipped anchor rows and 'The top of one sample, not a ceiling'.
6. Real-height mode adds 1 m, 2 m and 3 m wall lines (z-real-top.png). The tool opens on its own validation case (duo.jpg) rather than on the turnarounds.",
    "problems": "1. 'Where does Rex sit?' needs a long scroll. His figures are at y≈7,555 of 11,880 (about 9 screens). On the phone the rail marks are unlabelled ticks in a 14 px strip. There is no Go-to menu below 720 px, and nothing on the page says the tape can be tapped to jump, so that affordance is hidden.
2. The first phone screen spends about 250 px on a 6-item edge key before the reader has seen a figure. The key swatches use four different group fills, so the fill colour looks as if it carries the edge meaning.
3. The 46 px rail takes width from 3-up figures at 86 px, where the dashed and dotted edges are hard to tell apart at 1x. Rail labels are 9.5 px.
4. The page carries about 1.1 MB of inlined figure data. In headless Chromium, a viewport scrolled 1.2 s after load painted blank, and it rendered after about 3 s. That needs Ramer-Douglas-Peucker simplification before shipping, as the proposal itself notes.
5. The 'GEOMETRY' chip is outside the agreed status vocabulary. Gap stops are equal-height boxes, so their size shows only on the rail.
6. The sticky rail depends on 100svh inside the claude.ai frame, which is unverified."
   }

  "recommendation": "Build on the reader proposal (phone-first stops with a pinned to-scale rail). It is the only one where a phone reader with ADHD gets a one-line verdict at every step, readable type (nothing under 11 px except the rail numbers), full-word status chips, and correct copy about 924.

Fix its two phone weaknesses first:
1. Put "Jump to Rex and Ollie" in the lede, label the duo's mark on the rail, and add a visible "tap the tape to jump" hint or a phone Go-to menu.
2. Move the 6-item edge key below the first lineup, or shrink it to one line with a "how to read a figure" toggle.

Graft from the lineup proposal:
- Its hatched-floor gap tiles and the meatball disc at the end of the empty floor. These are stronger than plain hatched boxes.
- The landmark wall rules.
- A tap-a-figure drawer at H≈230 with per-part marking explained in words. Without it the edge marking cannot be read on a phone.

Graft from the instrument proposal:
- Its "Zoom 15 to 50" idea, for a to-scale lane of humans.
- The detail panel's girth-by-girth outline list and "What this ignores".
- The bench's PASS/CHECK chips with numbers and its ± column.
- The worked plain-FFMI-versus-score table.

Rules for the build, whichever base is used:
- Never write "no body can score above 924" or "nothing can score higher". The instrument mock does both, and the claim is false: a cylinder of the same height scores about 1.5 times as much.
- Default to all 49 builds, not "Key 20".
- Don't put an empty decorative log tape over anything that is not to scale.
- Keep every label at 11 px or more on the phone, including SVG guide labels (the lineup's are 4.1 px).
- Default the tool's height field to skull-top height, not 3.048 m.
- Simplify the inlined outlines well below 1 MB.

args.prompt:
You are reviewing "Build Comparison", a self-contained HTML page (claude.ai Artifact) in /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-comparison/. It ranks men's builds by a size-independent score S = 1.8 x fat-free mass / height^3 (FFMI the body would have at 1.80 m, same shape), from ordinary men to two original 3 m characters (Rex and Ollie), with silhouettes drawn from data, empty stretches left visibly empty, three "functional limits" found by geometry on widened template figures, a "meatball" end of scale (924), and a measuring tool for A-pose model sheets.
Read first: /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-comparison/BRIEF.md (the request), /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-comparison/research/reviews/design.md (the design spec and judges; skim), and the code: src/app.html (page), src/model.js (scores, body fat, gaps), src/figure.js (silhouettes, limits geometry), src/measure.js (measuring tool), tools/compute_limits.js, data/settings.json (copy, fat classes, stops, limits text), data/facts.json (research facts with verifier results; research/corrections.json), data/limits.json, build.js, test/test.js, test/duo.js, test/shots.js. Builds come from /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-calculator/data/builds.json via /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-calculator/src/calc.js.
Build: cd /home/user/rex-strength-lab/build-comparison && node build.js (writes dist/index.html). Tests: node test/test.js; node test/duo.js; node test/shots.js (writes shots/). Render the page yourself with Playwright: require('/opt/node22/lib/node_modules/playwright'); chromium.launch({ executablePath: '/opt/pw-browsers/chromium-1194/chrome-linux/chrome' }); wrap dist/index.html in '<!doctype html><html><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"></head><body>' + page + '</body></html>' and load it from a file. Google Fonts will not load without routing them through curl (see test/shots.js routeFonts); fallback fonts are fine for logic checks. window.__bc exposes LIST, GAPS, SEQ, HUMAN_TOP, MEAT, AX, sc.
The owner is a professional critic: factual accuracy and honest labelling come first (see CLAUDE.md, already loaded). Do NOT edit anything under /home/user/rex-strength-lab. Write scratch scripts and screenshots under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-rex-strength-lab/9b81b796-3162-56bd-85b7-22e02b6583e2/scratchpad/review1/ (create it). Every finding must be reproduced: give the exact input or place, what the page or code does (quote it, or the script output), what is correct with your derivation or source, and a minimal fix. Report real defects only: wrong maths or physics, wrong or unsupported claims, mislabelled status, contradictions between parts of the page, broken layout or controls, tests that do not test what they say. Skip style preferences.

Another reviewer (code lens) reported the findings below. For EACH one, try hard to REFUTE it: reproduce it yourself with your own script or browser run, independently of theirs. Mark real=true only if you reproduced it. Confirm the severity and give the best minimal fix (exact code or text). Default to real=false if you cannot reproduce it.

FINDINGS:
[
 {
  "id": "F1",
  "severity": "major",
  "title": "Limit scores are S(f=1) x f^2, not the widened shape read with the measuring tool as the page says; the hands-to-face band is about 30% too high",
  "location": "build-comparison/tools/compute_limits.js:8 and :62 (score: round(S1 * f * f, 2)), :72 (faceLow); data/settings.json limits.method and face.definition ('near 220'); data/limits.json",
  "evidence": "settings.limits.method (shown on the page): \"...until the limit is reached, and that shape's score is read with the measuring tool at 1,060 kg/m³ and 7.5% fat.\" The code measures only the f=1 shape, then multiplies by f^2 (comment: 'every width and depth scales by f'). Figure.human does not scale that way. Head, hand and foot sizes and the biacromial width stay fixed, and once the widened thighs cross the midline they are clipped there (Math.max(0, p[0])), as are arms that merge into the torso. Script scratchpad/review1/f2.js and an inline loop ran measureTemplate(id, 1.8, f, 800) on each limit shape. Median soldier: arms 42.4 -> measured 41.7 (-1.6%); thighs 48.9 -> 47.4 (-3.1%); face 217.1 -> 152.0 (-30.0%). Face for each template: p5 203.3 -> 142.6; p95 233.3 -> 162.7; Reeves 190.2 -> 136.2; Coleman 206.1 -> 151.1; largest arm 180.6 -> 132.1. Pessimistic bound (f 1.786): 86.1 -> 77.8. Thighs, Reeves: 53.2 -> 49.4 (-7.1%). So the published face band of 86-233 ('near 220' in the page text, '86 to 230' in the README) should be about 78-163. The shape at f=2.837 passes all of the tool's checks (scratchpad/review1/face-limit-shape.png). The test 'widening every run by f multiplies the measured volume by f^2' checks M.scaleRuns on a mask, not Figure.human's widthScale, so nothing tests the assumption compute_limits relies on.",
  "expected": "Each limit's score should be what the widened shape measures (the stated method). At the face limit the tool finds no arms and counts arm pixels at torso depth, so 152 is if anything an overestimate; the f^2 value of 217 is not that shape's score under any reading.",
  "fix": "In run(), set row[k].score = measureTemplate(id, H, f, 800).res.score.value (and do the same for faceLow) instead of S1*f*f. Regenerate limits.json. Replace the typed 'near 220' and 'near 90' in settings face.definition with values filled from limits.json. Add a test that each limits.json score is within 1% of measureTemplate at its f."
 },
 {
  "id": "F2",
  "severity": "major",
  "title": "A sheet with front and back views but no side view passes every check, and the back view is used as the side depth (score +29%)",
  "location": "build-comparison/src/measure.js:696-699 (views.length !== order.length is only a warning; V assigned by position)",
  "evidence": "scratchpad/review1/frontback.js renders the median soldier as front + back (no side) and as front + side + back. Node: 'front+side+back sheet: ok true volume 0.088 score 26.6 chest 107.7 cm' vs 'front+back sheet: ok true volume 0.113 score 34.2 chest 115.1 cm | errors: [] | view warning: Found 2 views; expected 3'. Loaded through the page's file input (odd_ui.js front-back-only): every check shows PASS, the view captions read 'FRONT · 602 PX / SIDE · 602 PX' (the 'side' is the back view), and the result is 'Score 34 31–37'. The 'treat these numbers as rejected' banner does not appear; the only sign is a NOTE.",
  "expected": "Front-and-back turnarounds are a common layout. The tool should refuse to measure depth from a view that is not a side view. Here the volume is 28% too high and the copy button exports it as a passing build.",
  "fix": "In measureSheet, set out.ok = false when views.length < order.length (or when V.side is missing by name). Also add a plausibility check: the side view's depth at the chest row should be clearly less than the front torso width (for example side/front < 0.9 at the chest and waist); otherwise reject with 'the view taken as the side looks like a front or back view'."
 },
 {
  "id": "F3",
  "severity": "major",
  "title": "Typed skull rows are not validated: a typo gives all-PASS results of 23,800,000 kg, or negative heights and girths; the overlay never shows the skull row",
  "location": "build-comparison/src/measure.js:709-722 (topOf, hpx, mPerPx), :760 (out.landmarks has no skull); src/app.html:1391 (reads res.landmarks.skull, never set), :1409 (rows only filtered for > 0)",
  "evidence": "On ok-sheet.png (a 602 px median soldier, ground row 649), set via scratchpad/review1/odd_ui.js. Skull rows '640': every check PASS, no rejection banner, 'Volume 22,425.244 m³ ... Mass 23,800,000 kg ... Score 6,800,000 ... Thigh 3,827.2 cm ... Crotch height 50.94 m'. Skull rows '5000': 'PASS View heights agree within 2%. Front -4350 px, side -4350 px, back -4350 px', 'NOTE The figure is -4350 px tall', 'Thigh -8.8 cm -7.9–-9.7 cm', 'Crotch height -0.12 m', 'Score 0'. drawSheet draws its blue line at res.landmarks.skull if present, else F.top. measureSheet never sets landmarks.skull, so the typed row is never drawn and the user cannot see the mistake.",
  "expected": "A skull row must lie in the top part of its view, above the neck and below the figure's top pixel minus a sane crest or horn allowance. Otherwise the sheet should be rejected with a clear message, never scored.",
  "fix": "In measureSheet, for each typed row, require V[name].y0 <= row < V[name].y0 + 0.15 * (V[name].y1 - V[name].y0); otherwise set out.ok = false with 'Skull row N for the <view> view is outside the head'. Set out.landmarks.skull = topOf('front') and label the gutter line 'skull' when ref is 'skull'."
 },
 {
  "id": "F4",
  "severity": "major",
  "title": "The target outline misses its target across much of the advertised 15-900 range (up to -34%); the copied JSON pairs target 900 with an outline that measures 590",
  "location": "build-comparison/src/app.html:1499 ('15 to 900'), :1513-1517 (one f^2 correction, then the final drawing with no re-check); test/shots.js only tests a target of 60",
  "evidence": "scratchpad/review1/target.js drives #tShape, #tTarget and #targetBtn in the page. Median soldier: 200 -> 'measures 190 (target 200)', 300 -> 290, 700 -> 640, 900 -> 760. Ronnie Coleman: 200 -> 190, 300 -> 270 (-10%), 400 -> 330, 500 -> 390, 700 -> 500, 900 -> 590 (-34%). 5th percentile: 150 -> 140, 900 -> 810. The cause is that the score is not proportional to f^2 once arms and thighs merge (same cause as F1), and the code makes only one correction step. scratchpad/review1/target_node.js iterates at the final 1,000 px with a secant step and converges: median soldier 200 at f 3.193 -> 200.0 (the page uses f 3.060 -> 187.9); Coleman 300 at f 3.331 -> 300.7; Coleman 900 at f 13.70 -> 900.0. text:
Round 1 is done and the round 1 fixes are live: the page is republished at the same URL. The pull request is open, but nothing is merged and Step 1 isn't finished yet. Review round 2, which re-checks every round 1 fix and looks for regressions, is still running in the background.

**What round 1 changed**
- **Limits:** the three limit scores are now the measuring tool's reading of the widened drawings, not a scaling rule. Arms forced out is about 41 (it was 42), thighs touching is about 46 (it was 49), and hands to face is 87 to 200 (it was 86 to 230).
- **Figures:** the same limit tests now run on every figure on the chart. Each figure is drawn with its arms just past where its outline lets them hang. Drawn from their own girths, the top bodybuilders already meet the first two tests, and the page now says so. The comic giants' arms come out nearly level.
- **Target tool:** it now lands within 0.2% of the target anywhere from 15 to 900. It refuses any outline its own checks would reject.
- **Sources and wording:** I fixed the source attributions, mislabelled numbers and overstated sentences the reviewers confirmed. The full list is in `build-comparison/research/reviews/round1.md`.
- **Measuring tool:** it now refuses a sheet that has a back view where the side view should be, and skull rows outside the head. It runs in the background, so a large sheet no longer freezes the page.
- **Accessibility:** focus outlines, screen-reader labels, the details panel at tablet widths, and contrast on the chart marks.

The reviewers found 76 issues and the checkers confirmed 69. Three are only partly fixed:
- **Contrast:** the light-mode gold for natural athletes is still too faint on the background. A darker gold would look the same as the bodybuilders' orange to red-green colour-blind readers, so this needs your palette decision.
- **Large sheets:** a 2,000 px sheet still takes about 10 seconds to measure. The page stays usable while it runs.
- **Tool start-up:** when you reach the measuring section, the target outline and the duo.jpg check still pause the page for about 1 to 2 seconds.

**Tests:** all model, browser and duo.jpg tests pass locally, and the Build Calculator's tests still pass. CI on the pull request hadn't finished when I last checked.

**Still to do:** fix what round 2 confirms, republish, then write the `history/` entry. A dry run of the history builder works and comes to about 5 MB.

**For you:** eight design decisions are listed in the pull request and in `build-comparison/data/NOTES.md`. Two are new from this round: the colour contrast above, and drawing arms at each figure's rest angle.
